acc-01.subject: One login in 100 days: where to start
acc-01.body:
Hi Priya,

Congratulations on the COO role at Harrowgate Lumen. Your promise of one login for every site is a bold one, and a good one.

One pattern worth knowing: most one-login programmes stall because teams start by rebuilding the directory. That work is slow and invisible to staff. The faster route is to join up the few apps people open every day first. For you, that means the three cloud apps. Every site then sees a real change well inside 100 days, and the directory work can follow behind.

No reply needed. I hope it helps as you plan.

Best regards
acc-01.matched_to: new COO, 1 September; first meeting point of view

acc-01.subject: The hidden cost of four logins
acc-01.body:
Hi Priya,

A second thought on your one-login goal. Four separate logins per person cost more than time. They drive password resets, which fill the help desk queue. They also leave leavers' access open longer, because each app has to be closed by hand.

A simple way to show early progress is to track two numbers each month: reset requests and the days it takes to close a leaver's access everywhere. Both should fall as soon as the cloud apps are joined up. They give your board proof long before the full project ends.

Nothing needed from you. Just something to use.

Best regards

A simple check helps. List the shared systems both sides will use from completion. Then ask who removes access in each, and how fast. Where the answer is unclear, that is where the day-one risk sits.

It is a short exercise, and it gives the integration team a clear list to work from.

acc-03.subject: Shared ward logins and the March audit
acc-03.body:
Marcus,

A second thought on the March audit.

Shared ward logins exist for a reason. Clinicians need fast access at the bedside, and a slow sign-in gets worked around. Wards that moved to named logins without fixing speed often slid back to shared ones within weeks.

The wards that held the change made the named login as quick as the shared one. They also started with the busiest wards first, where most record views happen. That moved the numbers fastest.

For Quillon's 6,300 staff, the order of wards may matter as much as the method.

Nothing needed from you. Just something to weigh.

Teams in your position often find that fixing who-is-who on shared devices gives the regulator the clearest story at follow-up. It shows you closed the root cause, not just the one hole.

A useful test before the season: pick one store and ask how quickly you could name the person behind a given refund. The answer usually shows the size of the risk.

Retailers who give each store worker their own login find leavers are simple to switch off on their last day. Head office already works this way at Lantergate, so the habit exists. It just stops at the store door.

One pattern worth flagging. ERP programmes rarely slip on code. They slip when contractor access cannot be granted fast, or cannot be proven removed at audit.

With contractor numbers up around 40%, every joiner handled by email and spreadsheet adds an account someone must remember to close. Over a long build, those stale accounts tend to sit on finance and operations data.

A simple check: pick five contractors who left last quarter and confirm each one's access is fully gone. The result is usually telling.

acc-02.subject: Fixing leavers before the build ramps

The cheapest time to fix joiner and leaver control is before the build ramps, not after go-live. Once data migration starts, auditors will ask who could touch finance and operations records, and when that access ended.

Teams that answer well usually do three things early. They give every contractor an end date at onboarding. They tie removal to that date, not to a reminder email. They keep one record of who approved what.

None of that needs to wait for the new system. It protects your Q3 2027 go-live.

The groups that handle this well do one thing. They bring every new practice onto one directory in its first month. After that, the access gets messy and the clean-up costs more.

It also speeds up integration. New sites get shared systems sooner, with fewer one-off fixes.

Nothing to do here. Just a pattern worth knowing.

acc-05.subject: Workstream 2 and the VPN
acc-05.body:
Kwame,

Your cloud RFP from 5 October puts identity at workstream 2. That order matters more than it looks.

Right now every one of your 4,800 brokers reaches client systems through one data centre directory and one VPN. If systems move to the cloud before sign-on changes, that VPN stays in the middle of everything. It becomes the choke point the migration was meant to remove.

Firms that sort sign-on early can retire the VPN on schedule. Firms that leave it late often end up running both for years.

Worth a look as you score the bids.

Best regards

acc-05.subject: Passwords multiply as data moves
acc-05.body:
Kwame,

One more thought on the migration.

Without single sign-on, each new cloud system tends to bring its own password. Across 4,800 brokers, that adds up fast. Help-desk resets climb. Weak and reused passwords spread. And it happens just as regulated client data is moving.

A simple check: count how many separate sign-ins a broker will need on day one after cutover. If the number is above two or three, the help desk will feel it first, and Celestine will likely hear about it soon after.

Happy to share how others have measured this.

Best regards
